title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
hook: is knowing about love the way to it? the sutras answer with a king and a meal
carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: love isn't only the road, it's the fruit, and the Lord is fond of humility, empty hands. Which trophy did you set down? Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

A menu can be a beautiful thing. Photographs, careful descriptions, a paragraph about the farm the tomatoes came from. You could read every word of it twice, learn it by heart, explain it to a friend, and walk out exactly as hungry as you came in. That small, familiar gap, between knowing about something and having it, is where the Narada Bhakti Sutras go next. Yesterday they placed love above the other roads. Today they ask the obvious follow-up question: fine, but how do you get it? Isn't knowledge the way in?
screen: `READING THE MENU.` → `STILL HUNGRY.` → `ISN'T KNOWLEDGE THE WAY IN?`

segments.voice: The sutras answer the way they did on the marks of love in year two: they let several voices speak. Some say, the text reports, that knowledge alone is the means to bhakti. You have to know who the Lord is before you can love him. Others say knowledge and love depend on each other, each one leaning on the other, like two cards propped into a little tent. Then a third voice, the sons of Brahma, whom commentators take to be the ever-young sages of the Puranas. They say bhakti is its own fruit. It isn't produced by something else. And here the sutras side with them, and give their evidence: it is seen in the case of a king, a house, and a meal. Then they spell it out. Knowing about a king doesn't make the king pleased with you. Knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger. You can know the palace floor plan and never be welcomed in. You can read the menu all night. So, the sutras conclude, those who long for freedom should take up love itself. Notice what they don't say. They don't say knowledge is bad, or that you should stop learning. Narada is, after all, a sage who knew a great deal. In the Chandogya Upanishad, which we read in year two, he even comes to his teacher with a whole library in his head and admits he's still not at peace. The sutras just refuse to let knowing about stand in for the thing. The king has to be met. The meal has to be eaten. The love has to be loved.
screen: `SOME SAY: KNOWLEDGE IS THE MEANS.` · `OTHERS: EACH LEANS ON THE OTHER.` · `THE SONS OF BRAHMA: ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `KNOWING ABOUT A MEAL ISN'T EATING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: from the menu to the meal. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind someone or something you love. For a few breaths, notice how much you know about them: their habits, their history, the facts. Then let the facts go quiet. Don't think about them now. Just let yourself be near them, the way you'd sit beside someone without needing to talk. If you pray, you can do this with God, setting aside what you know about God for a while. Stay with the nearness. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. For the sutras, its own fruit: knowing about the king doesn't please him, and knowing about the meal doesn't feed you.
Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. Today, trade one piece of knowing about for one piece of being with: call instead of checking their page. Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Narada Bhakti Sutras use the king and the meal to explain that devotion is something lived, not only studied, and pair the study of the text with worship, singing and service.

fork.setup: three views on how love is reached are set before you. which one do the sutras themselves side with?
options: knowledge and love depend on each other.
fork.reveal: they side with the sons of Brahma: love is its own fruit. knowing about a king doesn't please him, and knowing about a meal doesn't end hunger.

original.note: Sanskrit phala, fruit: the sutras call bhakti svayam phala-rūpā, of the form of its own fruit.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you learn enough about God, love will follow.
what it means: the sutras say love is its own fruit; knowing about the king doesn't please the king.
what a scholar hears: tasyā jñānam eva sādhanam ity eke, then anyonyāśrayatvam ity anye, then svayaṃ phala-rūpateti brahma-kumārāḥ: three views set side by side, and the text sides with the third.

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 28–33 (knowledge as means; mutual dependence; the sons of Brahma: its own fruit; the king, the house, the meal; so take up bhakti)

notes: Sutras 28–33 paraphrased. Sutra 31 names a king, a house and a meal; sutra 32 spells out only the king (not pleased) and hunger (not satisfied). The script says 'then they spell it out' and gives those two; the palace floor plan line is the script's own gloss of the house, not the text. Confirm.
'Brahma-kumaras' rendered as 'the sons of Brahma, the ancient sage-boys of the Puranas' (Sanatkumara and his brothers, as commentators take it). Confirm the identification and the description.
The link to Chandogya 7.1 (Narada learned but not at peace) recalls day 352; it is the same sage by name in tradition. Confirm the connection is appropriate to make.
The two-cards image for mutual dependence is the script's own illustration.
Editor pass: the identification of the 'sons of Brahma' is now attributed to commentators rather than stated as fact.
